query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a tailored surface modification treatment that promotes the in-situ formation of a stable, self-lubricating oxide nanolayer on a CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy will enable the alloy to maintain a consistently low coefficient of friction and minimized wear rate during sliding tests from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix without any surface modifications, which exhibits rising friction and wear at elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: A single, controlled surface modification treatment (e.g., a pre-oxidation or surface activation process) designed to induce the formation of a nanostructured, protective oxide layer during initial sliding contact.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted in ambient air over a temperature range from approximately 25 °C to 800 °C under varied loads representative of typical operating conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a nanolayer comprising self-organized, high-temperature stable oxide phases that are finely distributed on the alloy surface, which act as a lubricious tribofilm.
generation.mechanism: At sliding contact, the pre-conditioned surface rapidly develops a protective oxide nanolayer that reduces direct metal-to-metal contact. This layer, by virtue of its nanoscale morphology and high-temperature stability, mitigates adhesion and abrasive wear mechanisms. It provides a consistent lubricious interface by lowering shear stresses—even under the thermally activated conditions that normally degrade tribological performance—thus preserving low friction and wear rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified alloy, the treated CoCrFeNi alloy will exhibit a lower and more stable coefficient of friction and reduced wear depth throughout the tested temperature range. The beneficial effects should be observable at room temperature and maintained or even enhanced as the temperature approaches 800 °C.
generation.baseline: The starting CoCrFeNi alloy without the surface modification, which tends to show increased friction and wear at elevated temperatures due to tribo-oxidation and degradation of the native surface.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is limited to sliding wear tests in ambient air under controlled loads and temperatures up to 800 °C. Effects beyond this temperature range, in non-oxidizing environments, or under drastically different stress conditions, remain untested.
generation.uncertainty: The precise phase composition, thickness, and long-term durability of the in-situ formed oxide nanolayer are uncertain. It is also unclear how variations in the surface treatment parameters might affect the formation kinetics and protective quality of the lubricious film under dynamic sliding conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi alloy samples: one set will receive the proposed surface modification treatment and the other will remain unmodified as a control. Subject both sets to identical sliding wear tests in ambient air under variable loads at temperatures ranging incrementally from 25 °C to 800 °C. Use a standardized tribometer and ensure environmental conditions are controlled. The evolution of the friction coefficient and wear rate will be recorded during sliding.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (COF) at each temperature increment
Wear depth or volume loss after standardized sliding durations
Surface characterization (e.g., SEM, XRD) pre- and post-test to assess the nature of the oxide layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not show a statistically significant decrease in friction coefficient and wear rate compared to the untreated controls across the entire temperature range (with no improvement at both room temperature and near 800 °C), or if the protective oxide layer is not observed to form and remain stable throughout the tests, then the hypothesis will be falsified.
